Name: Ammon
Description: Ammon was the ram-horned oracular god of Siwa, combining Libyan and Egyptian religious traditions. The oasis sanctuary became an important source of divine legitimation, and Greek visitors later identified the god with Zeus. The visualization date follows the sanctuary’s securely attested prominence around the sixth century BCE; the cult may be older, but a third-millennium date cannot be supported.

Name: Gurzil
Description: Gurzil was a Libyan deity associated with the Laguatan of Tripolitania. In Corippus’ sixth-century account, he is called a son of Ammon and a cow, and his worshippers carry a bull-shaped representation into battle. This is the first secure evidence for him; proposals connecting the cult to earlier Neo-Punic inscriptions or to Ghirza remain disputed.

Name: Antaeus
Description: Antaeus is a Libyan giant known through Greek tradition. As a son of Earth, he renewed his strength whenever he touched the ground and was overcome only when Heracles lifted him away from it. Ancient writers later localized his tomb and memory near Tingis. The figure can therefore represent Greek engagement with Libyan ideas of land and autochthony, but the claim that he was originally a local deity named Anti is not securely established.

Name: Dido (Elissa)
Description: Dido, or Elissa, is the legendary Tyrian princess and founder-queen of Carthage. In the foundation tradition, she fled after her brother Pygmalion killed her husband, gathered followers, and established a new city in North Africa through the famous oxhide stratagem. The conventional date of Carthage’s foundation is 814/813 BCE. Her historical existence cannot be demonstrated, and Virgil’s later romance with Aeneas is distinct from the older foundation narrative.

Name: Tanit
Description: Tanit rose to prominence at Carthage by about the fifth century BCE and became one of the principal deities of the Punic world, commonly invoked with Baal Hammon. Votive inscriptions and the distinctive Tanit sign associate her with protection, fertility, communal continuity, and the welfare of Carthage. Her precise origins and the full meaning of her symbol remain debated, so she is best described as a distinctly Punic goddess with wider Phoenician connections.

Name: Mago the Farmer
Description: Mago was the Carthaginian author traditionally credited with a twenty-eight-book agricultural treatise covering estate management, viticulture, arboriculture, livestock, and other rural practices. His personal dates are unknown, so the third century BCE is used only as an approximate visualization date. After Carthage fell in 146 BCE, the Roman Senate ordered the work translated into Latin; Greek and Roman agricultural writers preserve fragments of it.

Name: Hannibal Barca
Description: Hannibal Barca was a Carthaginian general and statesman who led the invasion of Italy during the Second Punic War and defeated Roman armies at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene, and Cannae. Polybius and Livy preserve differing versions of a childhood oath connected with hostility to Rome, so the episode should be treated as an ancient biographical tradition rather than a certain verbatim event. After defeat at Zama, Hannibal remained politically active before exile and death in the eastern Mediterranean.

Name: Masinissa
Description: Masinissa was a Numidian prince who initially fought for Carthage during the Second Punic War before aligning with Rome. His cavalry contributed to the Roman victory at Zama, after which he united the Massylian and Masaesylian territories into a powerful Numidian kingdom. His long reign strengthened royal government, agriculture, and urban centers, making him the founder of unified Numidia even though his expansion repeatedly brought him into conflict with Carthage.

Name: Jugurtha
Description: Jugurtha was a Numidian prince, the biological grandson of Masinissa through Mastanabal and later the adopted son of his uncle Micipsa. After serving with Roman forces at Numantia, he fought his cousins for control of Numidia and became the principal opponent of Rome in the Jugurthine War. His resistance combined mobile warfare, diplomacy, and exploitation of Roman corruption. Betrayed by Bocchus of Mauretania, he was taken to Rome and died in captivity in 104 BCE.
